values.value: • Use the early entry to shape the deal before competitors define it. • Clarify why action is needed now and what happens if the issue remains unsolved. • Help the buyer define success criteria, owners, and first milestones. • Get close to the users and the decision maker while the buying vision is still forming. • Drive towards a solution framing that naturally favours your strengths.
3|Need
Buyer may say, 'We are at a very early stage.' Response: 'That is actually a good time to shape the right outcome and avoid a lot of late-stage correction.'
Good entry point. Push quickly into pain, urgency, and who owns the problem so you keep control of the deal.
Low risk. Build urgency while you have momentum.
Ask: 'What is forcing action now, and who is most affected if this remains unsolved?'
Need

• Convert interest into a real business case before the deal goes cold. • Find the underlying driver behind the stated want: performance, compliance, speed, quality, or visibility. • Test whether the buyer has urgency, ownership, and consequence for delay. • Sharpen the value proposition to specific outcomes rather than nice-to-have features. • Move the buyer from curiosity to committed evaluation.
3|Want
Buyer may say, 'This is more of a good-to-have.' Response: 'Makes sense. Let us test whether there is enough business value to treat it as a priority or keep it as a later initiative.'
Move this from interest to business need. Tie the ask to a measurable outcome, risk, or leadership priority.
Risk: 'Nice to have' deals slip easily.
Ask: 'What improves for the business if this gets approved this quarter?'
Want

• Do not assume a written requirement means high win probability. • Check whether the requirement came from a real need or from a standard sourcing process. • Rebuild influence by understanding pain, criteria, and political context behind the requirement. • Look for room to shape scope, sequencing, or buying priorities. • Position your offer around gaps competitors may miss.
3|Requirement
Buyer may say, 'The requirement is already frozen.' Response: 'Understood. I would still like to understand what sits behind it so I can align the response to what really matters.'
You entered after the need was formed. Re-open discovery and influence the criteria before you become a vendor in a race.
Risk: You may be too late and too comparable.
Ask: 'How were the current requirements decided, and where is there still room to shape the solution?'
Requirement

• Re-open discovery instead of behaving like this is only a final comparison exercise. • Find the decision criteria, hidden objections, and who is actually driving preference. • Ask what would make one option clearly stronger than the others. • Tighten your messaging around the few areas where the buyer really cares. • Do not rely on a generic demo or proposal to win late-stage evaluation.
3|Evaluation
Buyer may say, 'We are only comparing options now.' Response: 'That is exactly why it helps to know what will make one option clearly stronger from your side.'
You are late. Stop pitching features and find the hidden decision logic, buyer bias, and what will actually tip the decision.
High risk: Late entry with little control.
Ask: 'Apart from the formal checklist, what will make one option feel safer or stronger to the final approver?'
Evaluation
At what stage did we get engaged with this opportunity?
